exchange.said: Who's Vlastos? You mentioned him.
exchange.reply: Gregory Vlastos was a twentieth-century scholar of Plato, and in a 1973 essay he made the charge you heard just before this. He argued that Diotima's ladder loves people only so far as they are good and beautiful. So you end up loving a bundle of their best qualities, never the whole, flawed, one-of-a-kind person. He called that the cardinal flaw in Plato's theory.

exchange.said: And does Nussbaum agree with him?
exchange.reply: Partly, and the chapter gets to her in just a moment. She takes his worry seriously, but she disagrees with him about one thing, and it has to do with what Plato does next. I'll let the chapter lay that out.

exchange.said: Huh. So who's right, do you think?
exchange.reply: Honestly, I think it's a matter of reading, and the text supports more than one. Diotima's own words about despising a violent love of one person lean toward Vlastos. But the line about the lover still tending the soul he found leans the other way. The chapter doesn't crown a winner, and I'd be wary of anyone who says it's settled.

exchange.said: OK, go on.
exchange.reply: Right, Reeve was just finishing his answer.

exchange.said: [The listener tapped to ask something. The chapter is paused.]
exchange.reply: Mm? Yes?

exchange.said: This order of loves thing, is it like a ranking of who you should love most?
exchange.reply: Not quite, though people often hear it that way. In Augustine it's less about ranking people and more about ranking kinds of goods: loving a lower thing, like gold or a beautiful body, above a higher one, like God or justice, is where things go wrong. The gold itself is innocent; the mistake is in how the lover weighs it. Brooks used it more like a family-and-friends sort of ordering, so your instinct isn't off, but that's a looser use of it.

exchange.said: So where would your kids come, against God, in that ranking?
exchange.reply: I don't have kids myself, but I can tell you what Augustine would say. God comes first, and he wouldn't see that as a contest. A child is loved rightly when the love is ordered rightly, not when it's smaller. Whether that means you love the child for their own sake or as a step toward something higher is the argument scholars still have about him. The chapter is about to take that up with the father's letter in hand.

exchange.said: That sounds harsh. Did people in Augustine's time actually live like that?
exchange.reply: It does sound harsh, and some scholars say so too. Augustine himself didn't live like that. The chapter's grief scene is the proof: he was wrecked by the death of one friend. I can't tell you how ordinary people in his day lived day to day, and his teaching was a bishop's theology, not a household rule. Even he seems to have felt the strain, which is part of why it's still argued over.

exchange.said: What about monks, didn't they leave their families?
exchange.reply: Often, yes. Joining a monastery usually meant leaving your family behind, and some children were handed over to monasteries by their parents when they were young. But monastic life wasn't loveless. Augustine himself set up communities where people lived closely together, and he wrote a rule for them about friendship and sharing things. So the picture is more mixed than "they gave up love."

exchange.said: Do you think that's what Brooks wants, though? He seems like a family man.
exchange.reply: I can only go by what he did on air. What moved him most was Ames's words about his son's face, and that's a love for one particular person. When he used the order of loves, he used it as a theory of how ordinary people go wrong, like lying for money. I don't know what he wants beyond that, and I wouldn't guess about his own family.

exchange.said: Funny, my mum always said you can't love God and ignore the people in front of you.
exchange.reply: Your mum was in good company. That's close to a line from the First Letter of John, which says that if you don't love the brother you can see, you can't love the God you can't see. Augustine knew that verse well and preached on it a lot. The chapter is circling the same question: does loving God ever pull you away from the person in front of you, or send you back to them?

exchange.said: Yeah. OK, let's get back to it.
exchange.reply: Right, so, the definition itself, and who broke it.

exchange.said: So Diotima was Socrates' wife, right? That's why he listens to her?
exchange.reply: Not his wife, no. In the dialogue she's a priestess from Mantinea whom Socrates says taught him about love when he was young. Many scholars think she may be Plato's invention, a character he made up to give the speech some authority. Either way, Socrates presents her as his teacher, and that's why he's repeating her words to the guests.
